research.open_territory: No channel owns deadpan, cinematic, adult small-life comedy without words. The scout (five batches: 23 queries, 22 returned results) shows four naming camps. (1) Size words, owned by Minuscule and the AI mini-world and doll channels, which read as kids or AI. (2) Cozy mood words (quiet, soft, warm, rain, Ghibli), owned by the ambience wave. (3) Studio or school labels (X Films, X Animation, X 3D, X Studios) and curators (KIS KIS, TheCGBros, ESMA, GOBELINS). (4) Creator names (AJ Jefferies, SkyeWei, Aaron Blaise). Adult relatable animation (Lord Wojak, Low Budget Stories, SkyeWei's 'I'll Start Tomorrow') uses dialogue and meme or self-help framing. The wordless channels that have reached scale are all-ages (Minuscule, Shaun the Sheep, Mr Bean), and the few explicit wordless-creature series are tiny and kid-leaning (Studio S 'Whimsy Creatures', Pajama Moon). Open: names drawn from adult paperwork and the workday rather than from size or cuteness. Examples: forms, notices, ledgers, minutes, overtime, the night shift, the small hours, waiting rooms, rent day, the last bus, the 9-to-5, the lease, the payslip, the bureau or department, the out-of-office. Also open: dry, mock-official or cinematic phrasing (a deadpan title card, a film-noir or weather-report register) that implies smallness by understatement or scale contrast rather than saying 'tiny'. Coined compounds that pair one plain adult noun with one quiet scale hint (no Films, Animation, Studio, 3D, Tales or Toons suffix) would stand alone; nothing in the niche reads like that. Keep everything out of the storybook register (no whimsy, critters, little, pocket, pluck), since a child-appealing brand creates made-for-kids problems. Keep the brief's example characters (snail, pebble, ant) out of the name too, because each is already tied to Minuscule, Elen Pebble Animations, Turbo or the Immortal Snail meme. Spanish check: avoid words that turn diminutive or cute in Spanish (-ito/-ita forms, 'chiquito').

table.name: Modest Catastrophes
table.why: Handle @ModestCatastrophes (18 characters). The name pairs a big word with a small one, which is the channel's whole idea: disasters on a small scale for very small characters, like the commute, the interview or being let go. It hints at size through understatement, not through 'tiny'. Dry and adult with no cute tone, nothing bad in Spanish, and easy to spell after hearing it once. The handle is near the 20-character limit.

by_lens.reason: Best fit. My own brandcheck run printed CLEAR: YouTube CLEAR with 24 channels in search and none matching, modestcatastrophes.com available, and 0 live US marks. A web search for the exact phrase found no book, show, podcast or channel. The understatement carries the whole concept: a big word made small, adult and deadpan with nothing toy-like, so it stays safe under the made-for-kids rules. It suggests tiny scale without the word 'tiny', reads as a cinematic short-film anthology, and covers every episode type (rent, the interview, being let go, the wedding alone), so it will still fit in ten years. It is memorable and easy to spell after one hearing, and 'catástrofes modestas' is harmless in Spanish. It shares no word with any sister channel. Small minuses: it is wry rather than warm; 'catastrophe' in a feed could briefly suggest fail compilations, though 'Modest' undercuts that; it shares only one word with the UK sitcom 'Catastrophe', also adult comedy, which is not confusing; and the handle is 18 characters.
